meta.title: Propositional logic
meta.summary: Propositions, connectives, tautologies and equivalence: the logic that the set-theoretic proofs quietly rely on.
meta.overview: Propositional logic studies how the truth of compound statements depends on their parts. Truth tables give a complete, mechanical semantics, and logical equivalence lets us rewrite formulas. De Morgan's laws reappear here as the source of the set version.
keyQuestions: When is a formula a tautology?
Why is $p \to q$ true when $p$ is false?
How are the set and logic versions of De Morgan's laws related?

nodes.title: Proposition
nodes.statement: A **proposition** is a statement that is either true or false. Propositional variables $p, q, r, \dots$ stand for propositions whose truth value is not fixed.

explanation.intuition: Something you could answer with yes or no.
explanation.detailed: '$2 + 2 = 4$' is a proposition; 'Is it raining?' and '$x > 3$' (with $x$ unknown) are not.

nodes.title: Logical connectives
nodes.statement: From [propositions](def.proposition) $p, q$ we form $\neg p$ (not), $p \land q$ (and), $p \lor q$ (or), $p \to q$ (implies) and $p \leftrightarrow q$ (iff). Their truth values are given by truth tables; $p \to q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.

explanation.intuition: Connectives are the operations of logic, the way $+$ and $\cdot$ are the operations of arithmetic.
explanation.detailed: Each connective is a function from truth values to truth values, so a formula with $n$ variables is described by a table with $2^n$ rows.
explanation.pitfalls: $p \to q$ is true whenever $p$ is false. 'If the moon is cheese, then $1 = 2$' is a true implication.

nodes.title: Tautology
nodes.statement: A formula built with [connectives](def.connectives) is a **tautology** if it is true under every assignment of truth values to its variables.

explanation.intuition: A formula that is true for reasons of form alone, whatever the variables mean.
explanation.detailed: Truth tables decide tautologies mechanically, but the table doubles with each variable. For infinite sets of formulas, the [compactness theorem](thm.compactness) of the next part reduces questions to finite ones.

nodes.title: Logical equivalence
nodes.statement: Formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are **logically equivalent**, $\varphi \equiv \psi$, when $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ is a [tautology](def.tautology): they have the same truth value under every assignment.

explanation.intuition: Two formulas that always agree, so either can replace the other.
explanation.detailed: $\equiv$ is a statement *about* formulas, while $\leftrightarrow$ is a connective *inside* a formula.

nodes.title: De Morgan's laws for propositions
nodes.statement:
$
eg(p \lor q) \equiv 
eg p \land 
eg q$ and $
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q$ ([logical equivalence](def.equivalence)).

proof.idea: Compare the truth tables row by row.

steps.why: Each variable is true or false.

steps.text:
In each row, $
eg(p \lor q)$ is true only when $p$ and $q$ are both false, and so is $
eg p \land 
eg q$.
steps.why: Read off the tables for $\lor$, $\land$ and $\neg$.

steps.text: So the two formulas agree in every row, which is the definition of $\equiv$. The second law is checked the same way.

nodes.title: Excluded middle
nodes.statement: $p \lor \neg p$ is a [tautology](def.tautology): if $p$ is true the left disjunct holds, otherwise the right one does.

notes: Lecturer question: should the course mention that intuitionistic logic rejects this?

figures.caption: 1 is true, 0 is false.

applications.title: Simplifying a logic circuit
applications.summary: De Morgan's laws let a NAND-only chip implement OR.
applications.scenario: A board has only NAND gates in stock, but the design needs an OR gate.
applications.modelling: A NAND gate computes $\neg(p \land q)$. We want $p \lor q$.
applications.solution:
By De Morgan, $p \lor q \equiv 
eg(
eg p \land 
eg q)$, which is NAND applied to $
eg p$ and $
eg q$; and $
eg p$ is NAND of $p$ with itself. Three NAND gates make an OR.

quiz.explanation: $p \to p$ is true in both rows; $p \land \neg p$ is never true.

The correct law is $
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q$; try $p$ true, $q$ false.

quiz.prompt: How many rows does a truth table with 3 variables have?

quiz.answer: Only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.
